name: Sketch Pencil 14 Pose
notes:
BRIEF. sketch-pencil.json with the worn graphite modelled: same mechanical-pencil line, same tonal range, same paper tooth, but the facet is bound to the pen's pose instead of to the canvas. A stroke pulled along the barrel comes out a fine dark line; the same stroke pulled across it comes out broad and lighter, and the difference follows the hand rather than the page. Everything else in sketch-pencil's brief still applies and is unchanged here.

THE GEOMETRY. A used lead is a cylinder cut off at the angle it is held at, so the patch touching the paper is an ellipse: its SHORT axis is the lead diameter, its LONG axis is diameter/cos(grip), and the long axis lies along the barrel's shadow on the page — the projection of the pencil onto the paper. Sweep the pencil along that long axis and the mark is one lead wide. Sweep it across and the mark is the whole facet. That is the whole effect, and it is two settings: tip.angle bound to Pen Tilt, which in this engine (and in Photoshop's bVTy 3) rotates the tip to the tilt AZIMUTH — the direction the pen leans — and a tip.roundness under 1 to give the ellipse something to be narrow about.

SIZE IS THE LONG AXIS, WHICH IS WHY 14 BECAME 23. The engine parameterises an elliptical tip by its long axis and squashes the short one by roundness, so a 14px tip at roundness 0.6 draws a 14px facet with an 8px lead — a thinner pencil, not a worn one. The lead is the thing that must not move: at roundness 0.6 the size that keeps it is 14/0.6 = 23px. Measured, that lands the along-the-barrel line back on the current brush's 10px and lets the across-the-barrel mark grow to 18px instead. The panel now says 23px for a pencil that still draws a 14px lead; that is the parameterisation, not a resize. Resizing still works: both axes scale together, so the ratio holds.

TEXTURE SCALE DID NOT MOVE, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. sketch-pencil's note says to rescale texture.scale alongside tip.size. It does not apply here, because the physical lead did not change size — only the number the engine calls Size did. Paper tooth stays at 0.4, and at fixed geometry it takes the same 17% of the ink out of the mark that it takes out of the current brush's.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENTS SETTLED. The pose fan, at 0/30/60/90/120/150 degrees off the barrel with the pen laid over 45: 10/13/17/18/17/13px, 1.8x wide-to-narrow, and the probe confirms it turns with the pen rather than sitting on the canvas. The current brush measures 10/11/11/11/9/9px, 1.22x, fixed to the canvas — that 1.22x is its 35-degree facet caught side-on, and it is why the effect was never felt in the hand: it was there, but it was pinned to the page. Note that the along-the-barrel width is 10px in both. That is the design: the everyday line is the line this brush already had, and what the pose adds is the broad mark, not a thinner one.

TONE CARRIED OVER, MEASURED WHERE THE TWO CAN BE COMPARED. `measure` scales its own probe surface with tip size, so its flat-stroke numbers for a 14px brush and a 23px brush are not read off the same geometry; these were taken on one surface at one y, both brushes, stroke along the barrel. Peak alpha up the pressure ladder: 0.28/0.60/0.75/0.82/0.85/0.86 at 10/30/50/70/90/100%, against the current brush's 0.24/0.55/0.71/0.78/0.83/0.85 — the same curve, a shade darker. The paper tooth takes 17% of the ink out of both, so the tooth is doing exactly the work it did.

Build-up is the one number that moved: along the barrel, ink over 1/2/4 passes runs 0.691/0.756/0.835 (x1.21) where the current brush runs 0.559/0.750/0.857 (x1.53). Across the barrel it runs x1.68, better than either. What changed is not the tone but the edge: the falloff is 2.2px in both brushes, and it is a smaller share of a mark whose core is wider, so the first pass starts with less soft edge left to fill in. Peak alpha after one pass is 0.835 against 0.812, and both reach 1.0 by four passes. Working into a line still darkens it.

DO NOT TUNE THIS BRUSH AGAINST `measure`'s GRAIN NUMBER. It reads 0.084 here and 0.42 for the current brush, and neither is the paper tooth: for a mark this narrow the flat probe's band statistics are dominated by whether the two soft edge rows clear the 8/255 ink floor, which flips on a fraction of a pixel of tip size — the same brush measures 0.09 at 23px and 0.43 at 23.3px. Texture on against texture off at fixed geometry is the honest test, and it says 17% in both.

FACET DEPTH WAS SWEPT, NOT GUESSED. roundness = cos(grip), so the number is a grip angle: 0.75 is a 41-degree hold, 0.60 is 53, 0.50 is 60. Measured anisotropy runs 1.36x / 1.5x / 1.55x / 1.8x / 1.73x / 2.2x for 0.75/0.70/0.65/0.60/0.55/0.50, each with size set to 14/roundness so the lead stays put. The pairs that measure alike (1.5x and 1.55x, 1.8x and 1.73x) are the fan's widths landing on the same pixel counts, not a real plateau. 0.60 was chosen on the two things that are not measurement artifacts: it is 1.8x, which is the point where the fan reads as two different marks rather than one uneven one, and it is a 53-degree grip, which is where a mechanical pencil actually sits in the hand. 0.50 is there if the effect wants to be louder, at a grip laid over further than most people hold one.

WHAT THE ENGINE CANNOT DO HERE, SO IT IS NOT ATTEMPTED.
• The facet cannot deepen as the pen is laid over. Physically roundness should fall as the grip angle rises (the cut through the cylinder gets longer), and every Control in this engine — Photoshop's included — ramps its parameter UP with the input: bound to Pen Tilt, roundness is FLATTEST upright and ROUNDEST laid over, which is backwards for a pencil and right for a chisel marker held on its corner. So the grip is a constant here (0.60, a 53-degree hold) rather than something the pen reports. Worth re-testing against Photoshop before assuming the engine is the one that is wrong: our tilt-roundness ramp is a linear 0-at-upright to 1-at-60, Photoshop stores a tiltScale next to it that we write at a fixed 200% and never read, and 200% is exactly what would make cos(2 x tilt) reach flat at 45 degrees. If Photoshop turns out to flatten with tilt, this brush wants roundnessControl on tilt and the engine wants fixing, in that order.
• At zero tilt the azimuth does not exist — atan2(0,0) is 0 — so a mouse, or a stylus held dead upright, gets a facet lying flat along the canvas x-axis. That is no worse than the fixed 35 degrees this replaces, but it does mean the brush is only itself under a pen that reports tilt. Every probe in `measure` except the pose fan paints at zero tilt, so their numbers describe this brush pulled ALONG its facet, which is the narrow dark case.

REJECTED, SO IT IS NOT RE-TRIED.
• Angle bound to Direction, or to Initial Direction. It is the obvious way to get a direction-dependent width and it is the wrong tool: direction-bound, the tip turns to follow the path, so the mark keeps ONE width through every turn — the exact opposite of what a facet does. The facet must stay still in canvas space while the stroke turns around it. Only pose sources (tilt, rotation) hold still.
• Barrel rotation (Rotation / twist) as a second input. Physically it is real — spinning the pencil turns the facet — but the wear tracks the habitual grip, so the facet follows the hand's lean much more than the barrel's spin, and hardly any tablet reports twist. Tilt alone is both the bigger effect and the one that gets reported.
• Shrinking the tip back to 14px and living with an 8px line. Tried in the sweep; it is a thinner pencil that happens to be anisotropic, not a worn one.

TO CONFIRM IN PHOTOSHOP. That bVTy 3 on angleDynamics means tilt azimuth there too, and that its sign convention matches — if Photoshop's facet comes out across the barrel instead of along it, the fix is 90 degrees in tip.angle, and the number belongs in these notes.
